title: CCI imposes monetary and non-monetary sanctions on Agro Input Dealers Association, Agro Input Welfare Association for indulging in anti-competitive conduct
body_text:
The Competition Commission of India ( CCI/the Commission ) passed an order dated 21.08.2026 under the provisions of Section 27 of the Competition Act, 2002 ( the Act ) imposing monetary and non-monetary sanctions on Agro Input Dealers Association ( AIDA ), Agro Input Welfare Association ( AIWA ), Mr. Manmohan C. Kalantri and Mr. Arvindbhai Jerambhai Patel for indulging in anti-competitive conduct of cartelisation.
In this matter, the Commission determined that AIDA, AIWA, Mr. Kalantri and Mr. Patel have acted in contravention of provisions of Section 3(3)(b) read with Section 3(1) of the Act. Accordingly, the Commission, in terms of Section 27(a) of the Act, directed the OPs and their respective officials (Mr. Pravinbhai Patel, General Secretary of AIDA and Mr. Sanjay Kumar Raghuwanshi, National Spokesperson, AIDA) who have been found liable in terms of provisions of Section 48 of the Act, to cease and desist in future from indulging in conduct found to be in contravention of the provisions of the Act.
The Commission, after considering nature and gravity of the contravention along with assessment of mitigating and aggravating factors, also imposed monetary penalty amounting to Rs. 81,889 on AIDA, Rs. 3,92,269 on AIWA, Rs. 4,98,903 on Mr. Kalantri, Rs. 74,717 on Mr. Arvindbhai Jerambhai Patel, Rs. 9,177 on Mr. Pravinbhai Patel and Rs. 8,622 on Mr. Raghuwanshi, respectively.
Further, the Commission, in terms of Section 27(g) of the Act, also directed the OPs to organise a competition compliance training programme in order to spread awareness about competition laws and to promote a culture of competition compliance within their associations.
A copy of public version of the order passed in Case No.06 of 2023 is available on the CCI website at www.cci.gov.in .

enrichment.summary: The Competition Commission of India (CCI) passed an order on 21 August 2026 against the Agro Input Dealers Association (AIDA), Agro Input Welfare Association (AIWA), and two individuals for cartelisation in violation of Section 3(3)(b) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002. The CCI imposed monetary penalties ranging from about Rs. 8,600 to Rs. 4.98 lakh on the associations and named officials, directed them to cease and desist from such conduct, and ordered them to conduct competition compliance training programmes.
enrichment.context:
The Competition Act, 2002 prohibits anti-competitive agreements under Section 3, with Section 3(3)(b) specifically presuming agreements between enterprises or associations that limit or control production, supply, or distribution to be anti-competitive if they operate in the same market (horizontal agreements/cartels). Trade associations of dealers or distributors are frequently found to indulge in such conduct by collectively fixing prices, restricting supply, or boycotting non-member traders, which the CCI has consistently penalised across sectors such as pharmaceuticals, tyres, cement, and now agro-inputs. Section 27 empowers CCI to pass cease-and-desist orders, impose penalties, and mandate remedial measures like compliance training, while Section 48 fixes liability on office-bearers of associations found responsible for the contravention alongside the association itself.

This case is part of CCI's ongoing enforcement against cartelisation among trade bodies that restrict fair competition, particularly in sectors like agriculture where input dealers can collectively influence prices and availability for farmers. Such orders reinforce the CCI's role as a market regulator ensuring consumer welfare and fair trade practices, though the relatively modest penalty amounts here suggest a smaller-scale contravention compared to major cartel cases involving large corporations.

prelims_questions.question: Under the Competition Act, 2002, an agreement between enterprises engaged in identical or similar trade of goods that limits or controls production, supply, or distribution is presumed anti-competitive under which provision?
prelims_questions.explanation: Section 3(3)(b) of the Competition Act, 2002 presumes horizontal agreements that limit or control production, supply, distribution, or provision of services to be anti-competitive (cartelisation).

prelims_questions.question: Which section of the Competition Act, 2002 empowers the Competition Commission of India to pass a cease-and-desist order along with monetary penalties against contraveners?
prelims_questions.explanation: Section 27 of the Competition Act empowers CCI to pass orders including cease-and-desist directions and monetary penalties upon finding a contravention of the Act's provisions.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the role of the Competition Commission of India in curbing cartelisation among trade associations in India. Highlight the challenges in detecting and penalising such anti-competitive conduct.
Examine the significance of Section 48 of the Competition Act, 2002 in fixing individual liability of office-bearers of associations for anti-competitive conduct.

study_notes.reason: The release carries a testable factual core (specific Competition Act provisions and CCI's remedial powers) alongside genuine analytical value on how cartelisation by trade associations harms farmers and how CCI enforces compliance beyond mere fines.

prelims.point: Section 3(3)(b) of the Competition Act, 2002 presumes horizontal agreements that limit/control production, supply or distribution to be anti-competitive.
prelims.why_important: A frequently tested provision distinguishing horizontal (Section 3(3)) from vertical (Section 3(4)) anti-competitive agreements.

prelims.point: Section 48 of the Competition Act fixes liability on office-bearers/officials of a company or association, in addition to the entity itself, for contraventions.
prelims.why_important: Tests understanding of how individual liability is attached alongside corporate/association liability under the Act.

prelims.point: Section 27 empowers CCI to pass cease-and-desist orders, impose penalties, and direct remedial measures such as compliance training programmes.
prelims.why_important: Clarifies the range of CCI's remedial powers beyond monetary penalties, useful for distinguishing Section 27 sub-clauses.

prelims.point: CCI is a statutory regulatory body established under the Competition Act, 2002 to prevent anti-competitive practices and promote fair competition.
prelims.why_important: Basic institutional fact about CCI's mandate that could appear in a statement-based question on regulatory bodies.

mains.point: Cartelisation by agro-input dealer associations can restrict supply and inflate prices, directly affecting farmers who are price-takers in agricultural input markets.
mains.analytical_use: Useful for a question on how anti-competitive practices in agricultural markets affect farmer welfare and food security.

mains.point: CCI's use of non-monetary remedies like mandatory compliance training reflects a shift towards behavioural correction rather than purely punitive deterrence.
mains.analytical_use: Can be used in a question evaluating effectiveness of regulatory bodies' enforcement tools beyond fines.

mains.point: Recurrent cartelisation cases across sectors (pharma, tyres, cement, now agro-inputs) indicate a persistent governance challenge in curbing collusive trade association behaviour in India.
mains.analytical_use: Supports an answer discussing structural challenges in ensuring market competition and the role of trade bodies in facilitating cartels.

low_priority.point: Specific penalty amounts for each individual (e.g., Rs. 8,622, Rs. 9,177)
low_priority.reason: Precise figures are case-specific administrative detail with no independent significance for testing beyond illustrating penalty range.
Ceremonial/administrative detail not relevant for objective or analytical questions.
